directions: Plant divisions or nursery-grown transplants in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic, average to dry soil in a lightly shaded woodland setting; this species tolerates dry shade far better than its wetland relative Doellingeria umbellata. Doellingeria infirma is native to dry-mesic upland oak and pine woods of the eastern and southeastern United States, forming an upright clump of smooth, entire leaves topped from late summer into fall by loose, flat-topped clusters of small white ray flowers with pale yellow centers. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes, forming modest colonies rather than the aggressive stands typical of its wetland cousin, and works well as an understory accent in a dry native woodland garden. Its late nectar is used by a range of small native bees and flies at a time when few other woodland natives are still blooming.

Set out divisions or container-grown transplants in spring into lean, dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; narrowleaf white-topped aster is adapted to nutrient-poor sandy soils and declines in rich, moist garden loam. Native to pine barrens, sandhills, and dry open woods of the eastern and southeastern coastal plain, it forms an upright clump of narrow, linear leaves topped in late summer by flattened clusters of small white ray flowers with cream to pale yellow centers, similar in form to the more familiar Sericocarpus asteroides but finer-textured throughout. It is slow to spread and best massed in a dry, sandy native meadow or pine-savanna style planting where its late bloom extends the nectar season for small native bees and skippers. Once established it is quite drought-tolerant and needs minimal supplemental water.

Plant divisions in spring into dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Dixie white-topped aster is native to pine flatwoods, sandhills, and dry open woods of the southeastern coastal plain and, like its relatives, resents heavy or consistently moist soils. The species gets its epithet from its narrow leaves, which are often twisted or curled along their length, and it produces flat-topped clusters of small white ray flowers with yellow centers from late summer into fall atop wiry, upright stems. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a modest colony and is best used in dry, sandy native plantings, pine-savanna restorations, or naturalistic borders alongside other coastal plain natives. Its late bloom period provides nectar for small native bees and butterflies as the growing season winds down.
